blocks.heading: Protecting capital providers
blocks.text: Lenders and investors need reliable information about a business and the terms on which funds are supplied. Government can support truthful reporting, action against fraud and appropriate enforcement of financial agreements. A lender may also use agreed collateral: an asset securing repayment if the borrower defaults, subject to the arrangement. This is loan security, not a guard outside the building. Limited liability normally protects owners’ exposure, not the lender from loss. Protection can reduce deception and improve informed decisions but cannot remove ordinary commercial risk or guarantee repayment and investment returns.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Omi Tools seeks finance using inaccurate financial records. It also offers an asset as collateral. Truthful records help a provider assess cash, debt and risk; collateral may reduce loss if valid and sufficient. Neither a security guard nor a profit claim guarantees repayment.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain the relevant meaning of security when fictional Eha Repairs pledges equipment for a loan and also employs a gate guard.

The pledged equipment is loan security or collateral, potentially supporting recovery if repayment fails under the agreement. The guard provides physical security. Guarding the gate does not give the lender the same repayment claim or eliminate credit risk.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Consumers, capital providers and protection
blocks.text:
Fictional Nara Tools has incorrect product information and unclear financial disclosures. Verified corrections and accessible complaint handling can address both; management compares that approach with publicity alone. For part (b) only, management refuses correction and continues the same misleading conduct after complaints. Other facts remain unchanged.

a Evaluate the corrective approach at Nara under the original facts. [12]
b Evaluate the response after management refuses correction. Explain whether the earlier approach remains sufficient. [12]

a Verified corrections and accessible complaints address the stated information failures more directly than publicity. Check that buyers and finance providers receive the relevant corrected evidence, and monitor recurrence. b Refusal and continued misleading conduct show voluntary correction is insufficient. Escalate to appropriate investigation and enforcement under the stated protective arrangements, while consumer groups can provide checked information. The objective remains accurate information, but the response must change because cooperation and implementation have failed. Do not promise that enforcement guarantees every investment return.
